facts.claim: KDA's chunk kernels are slow because of an inter-chunk serial dependency
facts.value: REFUTED. Three independent measurements: (1) time scales LINEARLY with B*h (work-scaled 0.98 from B=8) -- a chain's latency does not grow with batch; (2) halving chunk_size to 32 DOUBLES the chain length and is 19% FASTER (T=4096: 12.12 -> 9.81 ms), the reverse of the chain prediction; (3) the genuinely sequential kernels (fwd_kernel_h grid 512, bwd_kernel_dhu grid 256) are 1.51 of 12.77 ms = 11.9% of KDA time. The real cause is OCCUPANCY: the four dominant kernels achieve 6-12% occupancy and run at 15-29% of HBM and 16-42% of SM, while every kernel above 80% occupancy runs at 85-93% of HBM peak. Grid size is ample (8192-131072 blocks on 78 SMs); the kernels burn too many registers/shared memory per block, leaving ~4-8 resident warps with nothing to hide memory latency. Latency-bound, not chain-bound, not bandwidth-bound, not grid-bound. Measured DRAM traffic: 14.79 GB in 12.77 ms = 1.16 TB/s, 29% of the 4 TB/s peak.
facts.source: eval/kda_probe.py@3d2acd9 plus ncu per-kernel counters

facts.claim: the fp8 quantize overhead is a second, transposed cast per tensor, and no torchao config removes it at a profit
facts.value: torchao 0.17.0 casts input, weight and grad_output TWICE per step -- once per GEMM, in two different layouts. The second is the transposed one, and it is 59% of the fp8 overhead (71.08 of 120.12 ms at batch 32; the four largest kernels in the group all carry _t_ in their inductor names). Float8LinearConfig exposes six cast configs for exactly this, and ROWWISE_WITH_GW_HP is the one recipe that removes two of them: it sets cast_config_input_for_grad_weight and cast_config_grad_output_for_grad_weight to ScalingType.DISABLED, so grad_weight runs in bf16 and its transposed fp8 casts never happen. REJECTED on arithmetic: the three GEMMs have identical FLOPs (all MKN), so moving grad_weight from fp8 to bf16 costs about a third of the 247.25 ms fp8 GEMM row at half throughput, roughly +82 ms, while the entire fp8 quantize row is only 60.93 ms. Even removing ALL of the quantize overhead loses. Separately it scales AXISWISE, which is what makes stock `rowwise` raise 'aten.clone.default with axiswise scaling is not supported yet' under compile on the AttnRes .chunk() path, so it is very likely unrunnable here as well.

config.use: A saving of x fraction of step time buys 1/(1-x) times the tokens in the same wall clock, so it is worth up to slope*ln(1/(1-x)) nat of quality. A throughput change that costs none (short_conv, an fp8 recipe) is a pure wall-clock win and keeps its full value as D grows -- there the conversion is 1% of step ~ 20 min per 34h ladder. Fraction of parameter ELEMENTS whose bf16 bit pattern is unchanged across optimizer.step(), by lr_scale: 1.0 -> 32.00%, 0.5 -> 48.38%, 0.2 -> 71.56%, 0.1 -> 84.19%, 0.05 -> 91.29%, 0.01 -> 98.26%. The schedule's own floor is final_lr_frac=0.05 with warmdown=0.65, so a run spends its last 65% of steps decaying into the regime where 91.3% of updates are discarded. bfloat16 carries 8 mantissa bits, so an update below ~2^-9 of a parameter's magnitude cannot change its bit pattern: it is computed, applied, and dropped with nothing raising. A stalled parameter is indistinguishable from a converged one on the loss curve, which is why this needed a bit-level count rather than a loss reading.

facts.value: The LM head's grad_weight accumulates in bf16, not fp32, and the resulting bias is real but harmless under AdamW. Recorded as a KNOWN PRE-EXISTING DEVIATION that the 15B and 30B numbers carry; b0 ruled it must NOT ship mid-run. MECHANISM. Liger FLCE has an fp32 accumulation path (fused_linear_cross_entropy.py:233-241, torch.addmm with out_dtype=torch.float32 into grad_weight) but it is guarded on grad_weight.dtype == torch.float32. grad_weight is zeros_like(weight) when accum_dtype is None (:76), train.py:1994 never passes accum_dtype, and our weights are bf16 (verified: head.weight and tok.weight are torch.bfloat16 in the step-7000 checkpoint, per t01's bf16-params-no-fp32-master decision). So the else at :257 runs: grad_weight += torch.mm(...).float(), rounding the running sum back to bf16 on each of the 64 chunks. SIZE. 64-chunk accumulation, bf16 vs fp32: median relative error 0.803% (b0 measured 0.75% independently), p99 33%, cosine 0.999954. WHY IT IS HARMLESS, which is b0's finding and the reason the fix is not urgent. The head is in the AdamW 'embed' group, not Muon (train.py:945 routes any parameter whose name contains tok or head there). AdamW divides by sqrt(v) and v tracks g-squared, so an error proportional to the gradient largely cancels in the update. What survives is a direction change, and b0 measured 0.146% sign flips on synthetic uniform gradients. B0'S FALSIFIABLE CONDITION, TESTED AND IT HOLDS. b0 flagged that their figure used a uniform magnitude distribution while real logit gradients are heavy-tailed, and said the ruling inverts if flips concentrate on high-magnitude elements. Measured with a lognormal per-row scale: unweighted flips 0.178%, |g|-WEIGHTED flips 0.0009%, and flip rate among the top-1% largest-|g| elements is 0.0000%. So the flips concentrate on near-zero elements, which is the opposite of the inverting case: the elements that drive the update are unaffected. THE DISQUALIFYING PROPERTY for shipping mid-run is comparability, not size. The head touches every token's loss, so changing its gradient accumulation between stages would confound every per-role row simultaneously, and unlike a reweighting it is not detectable per role -- prereg 7.1's gate is structurally blind to it. Fix path: accum_dtype=torch.float32, one keyword, 33.6M x 4 = 134 MB, after the 30B run completes, as its own change with its own A/B.
facts.source: train.py, facts/efficiency.json#eff.lm_head_is_compute_bound, docs/lessons/fp8_lm_head_design.md

facts.value: The recurrence is explained, from the probe log I already had: FlashAttention recompiles on an UNBOUNDED batch_size guard, so the variant set never closes and eviction is permanent. This answers the one open question in eff.recompile_reason_named and eff.steady_state_composition, and it partly un-retracts cu bucketing. HOW IT WAS FOUND. Correlating recompile lines against step lines in runs/t57_recompile.log by position: 202 recompiles total, 172 before step 10, then 12 / 6 / 3 / 5 / 4 in the step bands 10-20 through 50+. The tail does NOT decay to zero. Every one of the four after step 50 is torch_dynamo_resume_in__flash_attn_fwd_at_406, i.e. flash_attn/cute/interface.py:406, and NOT AttnRes.forward. So the late recompiles are a different frame from the 24 early ones I reported. THE GUARD, verbatim: '- 13/0: batch_size == 66  # total_mblocks = batch', then 78, 68, 85, 81, 61, 83, 53, and so on. 45 DISTINCT values appear across ~60 steps, spanning 43 to 116, which is 61% of that range. This 'batch_size' is not Cfg.batch=16: it is FlashAttention's varlen block count, which tracks the number of DOCUMENTS in the batch, and doc count is drawn from a distribution rather than fixed. WHY IT RECURS FOREVER. torch._dynamo.config.recompile_limit is 64 (train.py:1912). With 45 values seen in 60 steps and new ones still appearing, the set does not close before the limit, so dynamo evicts and recompiles indefinitely. That is the mechanism behind gaps containing compile_attempt_1 at step 260, which a finite 25-variant AttnRes set could not produce. Frame 13 is also the frame the live stage-1 run reports as hitting recompile_limit(64) on all 7 ranks -- an identification I had earlier flagged as open. BUCKETING IS BACK, on the doc count rather than on cu's length. Padding the doc count to a multiple of 8 collapses the 45 values to 10 variants, 16 gives 6, and 32 gives 3 -- all far under the 64 limit, so the set closes and eviction stops. This is why I only PARTLY un-retract: my original cu-bucketing proposal targeted mark_dynamic(cu, 0) at train.py:855, and b0 is right that mark_dynamic already gives cu one graph. The correct target is FlashAttention's block count, a different quantity in a different file, and the fix is not ours to make directly -- it lives in the flash_attn varlen wrapper.

facts.value: a second PROCESS cannot use a training card's idle SMs, and this is architectural rather than a tuning question. NVIDIA's MPS documentation (docs.nvidia.com/deploy/mps/architecture.html, Background, read directly 2026-09-01): 'Work launched to the compute engine from work queues belonging to different CUDA contexts cannot execute concurrently.' Without MPS each process gets 'a serially scheduled time-slice on the whole GPU'. So both the temporal and spatial idle in our step are unreachable by a plain second process; reaching them requires one CUDA context (streams) or MPS. MPS costs, from the same page: fault isolation is partial -- in shared-server mode 'a fatal fault from one client may bring down a different user's client that shares any GPU with the faulting client' -- and it documents NO memory partitioning, only per-client address spaces and 'limited execution resource provisioning for Quality of Service'. Measured primary degradation from a co-tenant: TGS NSDI'23 43% (ResNet-50 + ShuffleNet, A100), AntMan OSDI'20 5.2x (V100, Alibaba production), Zico ATC'21 8x (MPS under memory pressure), MIG 23% even with hardware partitioning, Gandiva OSDI'18 -13% as the best case and only for an already 94%-utilized job.

facts.value: empty SM slots are not fillable capacity, measured in our own occupancy regime. Elvinger et al. SoCC '25 (arXiv 2501.16909, H100, Nsight Compute instrumented) ran two kernels at 6.25% ACHIEVED OCCUPANCY each, separate CUDA streams, every SM available, and measured a 1.73x latency increase EACH. Naive occupancy math predicts no interference. Our KDA gated-delta backward sits at 6-13% occupancy, the same regime on Hopper-class silicon. Their diagnosis: occupancy is the wrong predictor; the binding constraints are IPC and warp-scheduler saturation, register and shared-memory capacity at the block scheduler, and L2/HBM bandwidth. Three specifics that transfer: a compute-bound kernel paired with a memory-bound one -- the textbook complementary case -- DOUBLED the copy kernel's time; head-of-line blocking occurred despite streams when a kernel needing 64512 registers/block found 63288 free per SM and the block scheduler serialised it (our worst KDA kernel runs 254 registers/thread against a 255 ceiling); and Green Contexts with strict SM isolation still showed 1.3x slowdown from L2/HBM contention alone. Ablation-isolated overlap gains across the literature are 1.05-1.31x, not the 1.9-2.2x of end-to-end headlines: NanoFlow's overlap term is 1.07-1.17x after a 13.2% nano-batching tax, Kernelet 1.05-1.31x with gains explicitly small when both kernels are compute-heavy or both memory-heavy, Domino ~1.2x. Flux goes NEGATIVE at small shapes on new hardware, -165% overlap efficiency at m=64-512 on H800.
facts.source: arXiv 2501.16909 (SoCC '25); arXiv 2408.12757 NanoFlow; arXiv 1303.5164 Kernelet; arXiv 2409.15241 Domino; arXiv 2406.06858 Flux

facts.value: our '95.44% busy' is a RESIDENCY measure and must not be read as SM utilisation. It is GPU kernel wall time over step span, the PROF_GR_ENGINE_ACTIVE family, which NVIDIA's DCGM documentation defines as 'the fraction of time any portion of the graphics or compute engines were active'. It says a kernel was resident, not that the machine was working. The gap is measured and large: Acme (arXiv 2403.07648, 4704 A100, six-month production trace) reports on the SAME clusters median nvidia-smi GPU utilization 97-99% against median DCGM PROF_SM_ACTIVE ~40%, and flags its own coarse metric -- "'GPU utilization' may sometimes be a weak utilization indicator" -- citing nvidia-smi as the reference. Consequence for any capacity question: derive headroom from ACHIEVED OCCUPANCY, not from the busy figure. Deriving our co-location spatial term from '95.44% busy so 4.56% free' would have been exactly the error this trace exists to expose.

facts.value: flash-linear-attention caps the KDA backward autotuner at num_warps [2,4] on Hopper, and our H20 inherits that cap, so 8 warps is never tried on the kernels that are occupancy-starved. Verified on the pod install, not read from a survey: fla/ops/kda/chunk_bwd.py:27 reads NUM_WARPS = [2, 4] if IS_NVIDIA_HOPPER else [2, 4, 8], and IS_NVIDIA_HOPPER evaluates True on our card (torch reports 'NVIDIA H20', capability (9,0)). The cap was written for H100, whose FLOP:bandwidth ratio is very different -- ridge point 295 FLOP/byte against H20's 37 -- so inheriting it by compute capability is an unexamined default rather than a tuning decision for this part. This is the first move of the KDA retune: one line, the autotuner does the rest, no numerics change. CORRECTION to my own first version of this entry: I recommended stepping num_stages down next. WITHDRAWN -- num_stages is also the cp.async multi-buffer depth, so lowering it frees registers and simultaneously REDUCES in-flight bytes, which is the quantity we are short of. It is a direct TLP-versus-ILP bet, not a free win. The right second move is moving load destinations out of the register file (cp.async/TMA staging), which attacks bytes that never should have been in registers, rather than maxnreg, which attacks the fp32 state accumulators that must be. Check n_spills at each point -- Triton's autotuner ranks purely by wall clock and will silently select a spilling config if it is fastest among a bad set. Calibration from Triton PR #9248: maxnreg gained 15% (2290->2640 GB/s) on H200 precisely because it did NOT induce spills; no published win comes from forcing registers down to raise occupancy. WHY OCCUPANCY IS THE WRONG TARGET: Volkov (GTC 2010) measured 87% of pin bandwidth at 8% occupancy, above cudaMemcpy's 71%, by carrying 8-14 in-flight float4 per thread. Same occupancy as ours, 3x our bandwidth. The machine demonstrably delivers ~87% at 8% occupancy, so our 29% is a register-budget problem and not an occupancy law. The measured record on forcing registers down to raise occupancy is one-sided: no published win. Triton layer-norm on B200 went 57-64us to 90us on an occupancy cliff with ZERO spills on both sides; FA2 varlen measured 19.6x slower at 32 registers versus 255-with-no-spill. NOT AN OVERSIGHT UNTIL PROVEN: fla carries no comment, issue or commit explaining the Hopper cap -- grepped in the installed package -- so it may be an H100 measurement or a compiler-bug workaround. Measure before changing, keep [2,4] as the control.

facts.claim: how much headroom a faster fp8 GEMM library could buy
facts.value: ZERO, not 2%: the fp8 GEMMs are already at ~100% of what this pod realizes, and the familiar '93% of peak' figure is measured against a VENDOR number the hardware does not reach. Two steps. (1) The 93% is arithmetic, not a kernel-efficiency measurement: eff.roofline_per_operator_prepad divides 67.8 TFLOP of GEMM work by 0.247 s to get 274.5 TFLOPS, then by the 296 TFLOPS of eff.h20_specs -- a vendor SXM spec sheet number, whose own uncertainty field already says 'realized peak is lower'. (2) This pod's realizable peak was MEASURED: eff.gpu4_peak_flops ran an 8192^3 bf16 GEMM and got 137.0 and 137.3 TFLOPS on two cards, against the same sheet's 148 bf16 -- 92.6% of vendor. Applying that same 92.6% to the fp8 line gives a realizable 274.0 TFLOPS, and the measured 274.5 sits AT it. So the 'library swaps cap at 2%' arithmetic (493.1 x (1 - 0.929) = 35.0 ms = 2.06% of a 1702 ms step) is computing headroom against a peak that does not exist on this silicon. The correct statement is that cuBLASLt is already extracting essentially all of the fp8 throughput this pod has. RETIRES THE LEVER BY NAME: swapping in a faster GEMM library -- CUTLASS, DeepGEMM, or any other -- buys ~0 on the GEMM itself. Note precisely what this does NOT retire: an epilogue that removes work AROUND the GEMM is a different lever and remains open (probes/t58_quant_tax.py@b15d348 measures 135.1 ms/step of quantisation traffic outside the GEMM). The two are easy to conflate because both are named 'CUTLASS'. AMENDED SAME DAY, assumption replaced by measurement: probes/t59_fp8_peak.py@fa8cc81 ran the same 8192^3 / 30-iter shape on the lane and measured fp8 at 279.6 TFLOPS = 94.5% of vendor, against bf16 136.7 = 92.4% (which reproduces eff.gpu4_peak_flops' 137.0 to 0.2%). So fp8 realizes a marginally HIGHER fraction than bf16, 2.1 points, and the carried ratio was slightly conservative rather than wrong. Against the MEASURED fp8 peak the fp8 linears' 274.5 TFLOPS is 98.2%, so the nominal headroom is 1.8% of the GEMM group = 8.9 ms = 0.52% of a 1702 ms step -- still under the 3% gate by 6x, and that is the ceiling for a PERFECT library, not a realistic one. facts.claim: whether 2x training throughput is reachable at 200M by changing the architecture
facts.value: NO on current evidence. Two independent paths, both capped near 1.2x, and they do not add. SOFTWARE: the four non-retired levers, every one idealised and all landing at once, sum to 158.4 ms of a 1676.63 ms span = 9.45% = 1.104x; the two with an established mechanism (fp8 head epilogue 75.5 ms, flash seam 54.9 ms) are 130.4 ms = 7.78% = 1.084x. SHAPE: holding body params L*d^2 fixed and respecting d %% 128 == 0 (hd=128, FlashKDA), the best shape is 2048x3 at 1.20x, because at fixed parameters speed is set by L*d and not L*d^2 -- going shallow-and-wide cuts per-layer bandwidth traffic and pays for it in a head that grows linearly in d. THE FLOOR: fp8 GEMM is 493.1 ms/step and immovable at 98.2% of this pod's measured fp8 peak, so even with head and everything else at ZERO the ceiling is 1676.63/(493.1+76.38) = 2.94x, and 2x requires the non-GEMM 1107 ms to fall to 269 ms, a 76% cut against 158 ms of idealised levers. THE PATHS DO NOT ADD: reshaping changes the same 917.2 ms group that KDA retune and fusion work target -- 2048x3 drops that group to 458.6 ms and halves KDA's absolute headroom -- so summing the two is double counting. WHY THIS REVISES THE EARLIER ~+30-40%% SOFTWARE CEILING: two items collapsed. fp8 GEMM library swap went 2.06% -> 0.53% because the old figure divided by a vendor 296 TFLOPS the silicon does not reach (measured 279.6). The fp8 LM head went +5.67% ideal -> MEASURED -3.91%, because the quantisation tax (135.1 ms) exceeds what fp8 saves on the GEMM itself (75.5 ms). What survives of the head is fusing that tax into an epilogue -- same block of time, different measure.

A is written by RMSNorm (train.py:240-247), also not a GEMM; the tool there would be a fused Triton RMSNorm-plus-quantise, not EVT. W is written by the optimizer once per step, which is a CACHING problem and is eff.fp8_weight_byte_cache. The CUTLASS facility itself is real -- Sm90ScaledLinCombPerRowBiasEltActAmaxAux emits fp8 D with a per-tensor scale and an amax -- it simply has no producer here to attach to. DEEPGEMM IS NOT A FALLBACK: its SM90 path is fp8_gemm_nt only with no fp8-output mode, it has no epilogue API, its README assigns fp8 casting and transposition to the caller, and its 1x128/128x128 block scaling is a DIFFERENT NUMERICS RECIPE than the per-tensor e4m3 that eff.fp8_head_activation_range validated -- adopting it reopens a numerics question already closed. Low: Liger's CE kernel cannot host a usable fp8 store, because a column-major scatter out of a row-parallel kernel is uncoalesced and costs more than it saves, so only the non-epilogue caching survives. High: every producer emits fp8 in its consumer's layout with no coalescing penalty and a delayed scale passes numerics. facts.value: A resume RAISES total_steps and the run RUNS the higher number -- it ends LONGER than planned, not shorter, and the extra steps read fresh rows, not repeats. Corrected 2026-09-02 after 44's review: the first version said the run stops ~78 steps short. That was backwards. MECHANISM: train.py:2436 computes total_steps from the plan in memory and :2445 adds resume_step back so step numbers stay absolute for the LR schedule. After a resume the plan is rebuilt from each domain's cursor (:1906 `used[name] = int(row_cursor[name])`), which allocates from pool depth rather than from what the ORIGINAL plan had left -- so the trimmed plan can hold MORE rows than the original allocation had remaining. Measured on p500m_20b_0902: 83 steps consumed 21,248 rows, the original plan had 4,861,564 left, and the rebuilt plan holds 4,881,604 -- 20,040 rows MORE. The loop at :2508 is bounded by len(Xtr), so it runs all of them: 83 + floor(4,881,604/256) = 19,151, exactly the total_steps the log prints. The run READS 4,902,852 rows against the original 4,882,812 -- but they are not all distinct. Corrected by de, 2026-09-02: 20,040 more rows are read, and that splits into 11,848 genuinely fresh plus 8,192 read twice. Distinct rows are 13,056 + 4,881,604 = 4,894,660. The 8,192 overlap is the single-segment cursor described in ds.second_resume_rereads_one_segment -- RETRACTED for current main by 52aec31 the same day, so the 8,192 overlap is a property of the code that wrote THESE checkpoints and not a prediction about a resume today; the cursor prevents a re-read only when its origin is 0, which holds for the first resume and not for any after it. INCREMENT: not resume_step. It is delta_step minus the difference of the floor divisions: 32 - (19,073 - 19,069) = 28, and 51 - (19,069 - 19,068) = 50 -- both observed. The naive form (floor of the trimmed remainder) gives 29 for the first and does not reproduce. NOTHING CRASHES: total_steps appears only in early-exit breaks (:2581, :2702, :2735); the rows and the step budget run out together by construction. The head of the run has the opposite sign -- a second resume RE-READS rows -- recorded separately as ds.second_resume_rereads_one_segment.

facts.value:
THE RUN-END CHECKPOINT'S ROW CURSOR CLAIMS 213,164 ROWS (0.87B TOKENS) THE RUN NEVER TRAINED ON, whenever --max_steps stops the loop before the plan is consumed. Two checkpoints of the SAME run, written seconds apart, disagree: ckpt_p200m_4b_0902.pt.ep1 carries row_cursor summing to 976,384 = 3814 x 256, the rows actually read; the bare ckpt_p200m_4b_0902.pt carries 1,189,548. The difference is 213,164 rows. A resume from the bare checkpoint would start each domain past rows it was never trained on and skip them silently.

MECHANISM, and it is a two-line interaction. train.py:2561 calls save_checkpoint WITHOUT a step, and :1034 reads a missing step as `no step (run-end save): the plan is complete` and writes the plan-complete counts. That reading was true when it was written -- reaching the end of the loop did mean reaching the end of the plan. It stopped being true when --max_steps was used to bound a resume: :2151 caps total_steps, :2520 breaks at `step >= total_steps`, and the plan still holds the rows the cap excluded. So the run-end save states a FACT (no step was passed) and the branch draws an INFERENCE from it (therefore the plan finished), in one line, with the inference recorded as data. The .ep1 save at :2545 passes step and is correct, which is why the same run holds both numbers.

ARITHMETIC. Segment 1 read 832 x 256 = 212,992 rows; segment 2 read (3814 - 832) x 256 = 763,392; total 976,384, matching .ep1 exactly. The bare checkpoint's 1,189,548 = 212,992 + 976,556, i.e. segment 1's rows plus the WHOLE second plan -- which is also why it exceeds the 4.00B budget: 976,556 rows was the over-allocated plan (eff.resume_inflates_total_steps), and 26,645 of the 122,069 rows per rank went unread.

SCOPE: any run that ends via --max_steps rather than by consuming its plan. Not specific to a resume -- a fresh run with --max_steps has the same shape -- but a resume is where it costs something, because a resume is the only consumer of the cursor.

    [32773,32784)          6.6575      0.0000       7.1036      0.0000       0.7302

update_geometry_step8000.mechanism_retracted: b0 first read the 28x momentum as 'pushed hard in alternating directions'. Muon's mb is an EMA (momentums.lerp_(grads, 1-momentum), momentum 0.95, train.py:578), so alternating gradients make it SMALL; a large mb means gradients are consistently aligned. And ||mb|| does not set the step at all -- the update is the Newton-Schulz orthogonalised X (train.py:592), whose norm depends only on shape, so 28x momentum moves the weight exactly as far as 1x. A card-minutes gradient-sign experiment was planned on that reading and was cancelled: the EMA has already averaged the thing it would have measured.
